job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Yusuf Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house in Calder Park with two other guys, one a nurse and one a trainee electrician, so mornings are a queue for the shower. Then I'm at the desk by nine doing applications, with a break at eleven for a run. Afternoons I do mock interviews with a friend from uni, and some evenings I drive for a food delivery app to cover my share of the rent. It's not glamorous, but it's honest money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what were your internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did finance and economics and came out top of my year. One internship was in the credit risk team of a mid-sized bank, Halvorsen Trust, where I cleaned data and built a few charts. The other was in the back office of a small asset manager, doing reports for clients. I also captained my university's five-a-side team, which I mention in interviews because it shows I can organise people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. Tools make spreadsheets quicker, and that's about it. I'd tell my housemates not to quit their trades to learn prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my own problem would be the same as today: I've got no offer. I have some debt, about two months saved, and my parents could help in a pinch, though I'd rather not. A quiet AI world wouldn't make banks hire any faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying to the banks' graduate schemes and also smaller asset managers, ten a week. I'd finish the professional finance exam I started, since it shows commitment. And I'd keep the delivery shifts, three evenings a week, so I'm not eating into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly because I want to stop driving someone's takeaway and start a real career. It's not the world that's hard, it's waiting. Running helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your first interview question to a bank be if you could ask anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the banks how many graduates they took last year and how many they'll take next year. If they won't say, that tells me something. I'd rather know than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long can you keep driving deliveries alongside job hunting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As long as I need to, honestly. It's about fourteen hours a week, and the bike is fine. If I get an offer I'd stop in a day. If I don't, I can keep it up for a year, though my legs would complain.

say: I'd say tools make spreadsheets **quicker** and that's about it.
I'd tell my housemates not to quit their trades to learn **prompts**.
think: My problem is the same as today: **no offer**, some debt and about two months saved.
A quiet AI world wouldn't make banks **hire faster**.
do: Apply to **bank schemes** and smaller asset managers, ten a week.
Finish the **professional finance exam** I started, to show commitment.
Keep three evening **delivery shifts** a week so savings stay put.
feel: **Uneasy**, mainly because waiting is hard when I want a real career.

fieldNote: Yusuf treats the job search as a **project** with weekly targets and a delivery-income buffer.
His question to banks about graduate numbers shows a numbers-first mind.
Mood is anxious not uneasy because there is no offer and rent is partly paid by app income.

steps.text: Apply to ten bank and asset manager graduate schemes a week
Finish the professional finance exam I started
Keep three evening delivery shifts a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say banks will use it for the checking and the first-draft reports, and they'll hire fewer juniors. I'd tell friends to learn the tools now, not later. And I'd say regulators should check the models, because a bad model with a bank's name on it is dangerous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried that the training ground for my career is shrinking. The cleaning-data and report-building jobs are the ones I did, and they're exactly what a tool does well. I'm top of my class, but so is half of the applicant pool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more, not just now and then. I'd learn one coding tool, SQL or Python, properly, so I can be someone who checks the model rather than someone the model replaces. I'd also ask my old team at Halvorsen Trust whether they have any contract work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but motivated. It's like the first week of training when everyone's fitter than you. You can either quit or catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of credit risk work do you think are already automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pulling and cleaning data, building first charts, and writing summaries for credit committees. At Halvorsen Trust I spent a lot of time on that, and one of the senior analysts told me he'd rather have a tool do it. He wasn't being cruel, he was being honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you decide when a tool is proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When two or three people I respect have used it for a few months and haven't had embarrassing mistakes. I used to be too slow, and I've caught up on some. I don't need to be first with a new tool, but I don't want to be last.

say: I'd say banks will hire **fewer juniors**, so friends should learn the tools now.
I'd say regulators should check the **models**, because a bad one with a bank's name is dangerous.
think: The **training ground** for my career is shrinking, because tools do data cleaning and reports.
I'm top of my class, but so is half of the **applicant pool**.
do: Learn **SQL or Python** properly to become the person who checks the model.
Use AI tools **daily** for data cleaning and summaries.
Ask my old team at **Halvorsen Trust** about contract work.
feel: **Anxious but motivated**, like the first week of training when everyone is fitter.
S1.quote: I don't need to be first with a new tool, but I don't want to be last.
fieldNote: Yusuf's **steady** profile shows: he waits for peers to prove a tool, then commits.
He names exactly which internship tasks are at risk, so his anxiety is specific.
Wants to move from doing checks to checking the model.

steps.text: Learn SQL properly through a free online course
Use an AI assistant daily for data cleaning and summaries
Ask my old team at Halvorsen Trust about contract work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is bigger than any one of us, and we should watch how governments respond. I'd want some kind of public support to cover the transition, because markets alone won't. I'd say it calmly, though I wouldn't feel calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think My banking career could close before it opens. Banks would move fast to cut costs, and juniors are the easiest cut. I'd be one of thousands of graduates in the same boat, plus all the people already working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: stop the gym, stop eating out, and move my savings somewhere safe. I'd do more delivery shifts while that kind of work lasts, since robots for the hands-on stuff come later. And I'd apply widely, including public bodies and any firm that still wants a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be sleeping badly and thinking about the maths every night. But I'd also feel a weird focus, because there'd be nothing to wait for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your housemates that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my housemates we should keep the house together and share meals, because cheaper is better. Dev, the electrician, would probably be okay for longer, and I'd feel a bit jealous. I'd say we should all check in on each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare penny into rent and keep a month in reserve. If I could, I'd go and stay with my parents for a while. It'd feel like going backwards, but I'd do it before getting into debt.

say: I'd say it's bigger than any one of us and **public support** is needed.
I'd say it **calmly**, though I wouldn't feel calm.
think: My banking career could **close before it opens**, since juniors are the easiest cut.
I'd be one of **thousands** of graduates in the same boat.

Apply to **public bodies** and any firm still wanting a person.
S2.quote: My banking career could close before it opens.
fieldNote: Yusuf's reading is **rational**: juniors are the easiest cost to cut, and thousands compete.

Fallback to his parents' home is a last resort and he says so.

steps.text: Cut the gym and eating out to save on rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to act, and we shouldn't waste it arguing. I'd tell friends to build skills that are hard to copy: judgement, relationships, being the person who signs. I'd also say governments should start pilot schemes now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but with a path. The warning lets me get qualified, get one or two jobs, and be a trusted person before the change. It's not a guarantee, but it's a fighting chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the first job as fast as possible and ask to work with whichever team is rolling out tools. I'd sit the professional exams, learn SQL properly, and save at least a third of my pay. And I'd keep in touch with everyone I meet, because relationships are what a tool can't replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd say it's the useful kind. I'd have a deadline, and I do better with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and take the delivery work longer, perhaps a year. After that I'd consider a master's in data or finance, if my parents can help with costs. I wouldn't wait forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if the first job doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A degree, a start in the industry and a bit of money, before the big shift. That's what five years buys. I can't promise it works, but the odds are better than with two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to adapt, but not if we all assume it's far off. Schools, banks and governments should plan now. I'd tell my friends to spend a year learning something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly okay. I'd have time for a career, a deposit for a flat, maybe a family. I'd still feel pressure to use the decade well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the first job and qualify, then move toward risk or data roles where tools are part of the job. I'd stay in touch with the delivery drivers' group, just in case. And I'd put money in an index fund every month, to have something that isn't wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. It's the world I could plan for, and I'd feel like an adult in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A career with a few promotions, a flat, and perhaps starting a small firm with a friend. Ten years lets me do it in order instead of all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd waste the decade and be caught out anyway. Or that the banks cut juniors long before 2036, so the first rungs go early. I'd watch hiring numbers as the real signal.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years doesn't give a graduate time to build a record, and I'd be competing with people who have ten years' experience and suddenly no job. What would help is a mix: some public support for the transition, firms being honest about what they plan, and a real way to get experience even if the jobs shrink.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people think graduates like me are lazy about tools, or that we're all panicking. It's more mixed. I'm cautious, but I'm trying, and I'd like to be judged on how I adapt.

headlineQuote: I'm cautious, but I'm trying, and I'd like to be judged on how I adapt.
portrait: **Yusuf** is a 23-year-old finance graduate, top of his class, sharing a rented house and driving deliveries for rent.
He is **pragmatic and centrist**, uses AI now and then, and adopts tools once others have shown they work.
His internships in **credit risk** and fund reports are the work he knows software is already reaching.
He tends to **move in steady steps**, with qualifications, networking and savings, not big gambles.
His mood climbs from anxious to alarmed in the 2-year world, then eases as time grows.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, because two years gives no time to build a record before experienced people flood the market.
whatWouldHelp: **Public support** for the transition and firms being honest about their plans.
A real route to **experience** even if entry jobs shrink.
